name: Ahidous

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: An experienced Amazigh community member or cultural educator.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Ahidous is performed at festivals, weddings, naming ceremonies, and after the harvest.
It serves as a social space for community interaction and a celebration of tribal unity and victory.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:Ahidous - Wikicamp Morocco 2023 - 2.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c8/Ahidous_-_Wikicamp_Morocco_2023_-_2.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers stand shoulder to shoulder in a circle, semicircle, or two facing lines.
The movement is collective, involving rhythmic stomping, trembling, and large, undulating motions.
Participants move in unison, creating a visual effect of juxtaposition where everyone performs the same gesture simultaneously.
Watch for Collective Undulation.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (8VbcXz-o2G4)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Circle, semicircle, or two facing lines.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is accompanied by the bendir, also called alloun, a frame drum, and the rhythmic clapping of the dancers.
Vocal accompaniment consists of songs in the Berber language, izli or izlan, though some tribes in the Taza corridor use Arabic.
Listen for the Bendir, alloun.
The sound is defined by the steady, resonant beat of the bendir frame drum, punctuated by the rhythmic clapping of the dancers and the communal singing of traditional Berber chants.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Men typically wear a white djellaba and a turban.
Women wear white or colorful kaftans, often accessorized with silver jewelry.
It is performed in village squares, at festivals, and during weddings.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Ahidous is practiced across the Middle and High Atlas, including provinces like Khenifra, Azrou, Ifrane, Beni Mellal, and Midelt.
The dance is linked to the Amazigh people and is often compared to the Ahwash of the Western Atlas.
